etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English subscriben, subskryben, from Latin subscrībere. Compare its native English equivalent underwrite.

definitions.definition: (ergative) To sign up to have copies of a publication, such as a newspaper or a magazine, delivered for a period of time.
To pay for the provision of a service, such as Internet access, a cell phone plan, or a streaming service.
To believe or agree with a theory or an idea [with to].
To pay money to be a member of an organization.
(intransitive) To contribute or promise to contribute money to a common fund.

quote.text: […]  under no circumstances could I ever again be nominated for any public office, as no corporation would subscribe to a campaign fund if I was on the ticket, and that they would subscribe most heavily to beat me;

definitions.definition: (transitive) To promise to give, by writing one's name with the amount.
(business and finance) To agree to buy shares in a company.

quote.citation: 1776, Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations:
quote.text: The capital which had been subscribed to this bank, at two different subscriptions, amounted to one hundred and sixty thousand pounds, of which eighty per cent only was paid up.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To sign; to mark with one's signature as a token of consent or attestation.

quote.text: [E]very officer who shall hereafter be appointed, shall, before he enters on the duties of his office, subscribe these rules and regulations.

quote.citation: 1855, Henry Hart Milman, History of Latin Christianity‎[1]:
quote.text: All the bishops subscribed the sentence.

definitions.definition: (archaic outside law) To write (one’s name) at the bottom of a document; to sign (one's name).

quote.citation: c. 1510, Thomas More, The Life of Pico della Mirandola:

quote.text: […]  although the will is holographic, and a holographic instrument cannot be admitted to probate where testator told the subscribing witnesses that it was not his will,  […]

quote.citation: 1957, Estates of Incompetent Veterans: Hearings Before the United States House Committee on Veterans' Affairs, page 1968:
quote.text: Commission to take testimony: testimony of subscribing witnesses may be taken by commission  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To sign away; to yield; to surrender.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Measure for Measure”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: Admit no other way to save his life , (As I subscribe not that, nor any other, But in the loss of question)  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To yield; to admit to being inferior or in the wrong.
(obsolete, transitive) To declare over one's signature; to publish.

quote.citation: 1598–1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “Much Adoe about Nothing”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii]:
quote.text: I will subscribe him a coward.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To indicate interest in the communications made by a person or organization.
(intransitive, programming) To register for notifications about an event or similar.
